originality.rationale: Primary arXiv:2603.18801v1/v2 introduce this precise evolving-infectivity SIR equation, discuss early-time Gaussian selection and policy-dependent finite-threshold attack rates; they do not state the global exact half-line susceptible extinction and bounded-domain sharp final size/noncommutation. Alfaro–Carles 2014 establish linear-fitness replicator-mutator acceleration but not a susceptible–recovered SIR terminal-size theorem. Broad heterogeneous-SEIR final-size literature was compared by statement, with unavailable full text documented as genuine residual risk. Eight actual semantic queries against published mathematical records and targeted primary-literature queries exposed no dominating theorem; lack of search hits alone was not used to infer uniqueness.
residual_risks: Almeida et al. 2020/2021 full primary text was not accessible; a specialist could uncover a more general implication requiring comparison. The inspected description is not identical to a pathogen-strain mutation flow.
The general 2025 trait-structured model uses bounded trait intervals; whether other modifications of its framework imply related unbounded-domain consequences is not established.
Public literature and database searches are incomplete discovery tools; unpublished work outside inspected sources cannot be ruled out.

value.rationale: The motivating 2026 evolving-infectivity SIR article uses effectively unbounded trait diffusion for early-time analysis, finite trait numerical implementations, and prevalence cutoffs for final attack estimates. The exact infinite-time continuum model has a singular, domain-dependent terminal epidemic size: any positive mutation diffusion can force total mathematical eventual infection on the unbounded rate half-line, whereas a physically bounded infectivity trait gives a strictly positive universal sharp susceptible lower bound. This precisely locates why long-time continuum extrapolation and capped numerical epidemic outcomes may disagree and why arbitrarily small mutation cannot be treated as a regular perturbation. The bounded-case inequality is classical alone, but it is the comparison half of an analytically new domain/zero-diffusion singularity rather than an isolated textbook estimate; no epidemiological policy prediction is claimed.
